title: The Rapid Adoption of Generative AI
author: Alexander Bick · Adam Blandin · David J. Deming

st.t: Aggregate productivity: Task speedups shrink during scaling
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s central proposition by distinguishing widespread adoption and reported task-level time savings from realised aggregate productivity. Its 1.1% estimate is explicitly conditional on saved time becoming additional production, while informal use, leisure, organisational adjustment and heterogeneous adoption may prevent potential gains from appearing in output statistics. It does not materially address employment reallocation.
qs: However, labor productivity gains will only translate into aggregate productivity gains if firms adjust their expectations.
Its economic impact will ultimately be determined by how many people use it, how intensively they use it, and the productivity gains it provides.

st.t: Knowledge work: Task gains do not ensure skill growth
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s distinction between observed AI use and established productivity effects. It documents low-intensity workplace adoption and derives only a potential aggregate gain from self-reported time savings and a production model, while leaving longer-run effects uncertain; it does not address durable skill growth directly.
qs: Combining detailed data on the frequency and intensity of genAI usage, we estimate that between 1 and 5 percent of total work hours in the previous week were spent using genAI.
Combining these figures with a standard model of aggregate production suggests a potential productivity gain from genAI adoption of around 1.1%.

st.t: Legal workflows: Immediate gains create competence risks
st.an: The source supports the synthesis’s cautious account of immediate but uneven gains: generative AI is used mainly for bounded information and writing tasks, workplace use remains limited, and self-reported time savings indicate potential rather than demonstrated aggregate productivity. It also reinforces the distinction between technical exposure and realised legal adoption, while not addressing verification or apprenticeship risks directly.
qs: At the same time, managers have relatively high adoption rates relative to predicted exposure, while legal and social services and office and administration occupations have relatively low adoption rates.
We estimate a mean time savings of 5.4 percent among all genAI work users, which implies a mean time savings of 1.4 percent among all workers (including non-users).

kp.k: Evidence measures economy-wide adoption, not legal-sector restructuring
kp.d: Bick, Blandin and Deming report U.S. generative AI adoption using the Real-Time Population Survey (RPS), principally pooling August and November 2024 waves with 5,014 and 5,329 responses respectively. The online Qualtrics panel is not a random population sample; the researchers target demographic groups and weight responses against the Current Population Survey (CPS). The final analytical samples shown in Figure 2 contain 9,742 adults aged 18–64 and 6,951 employed respondents. This is a working paper, not peer-reviewed evidence. Legal occupations appear within a combined legal/social services group rather than a dedicated legal-services study.
qs: The Qualtrics panel includes about 15 million members and is not a random sample of the U.S. population.
We then launched the full genAI module with the August and November 2024 waves and received 5,014 and 5,329 responses respectively.
They have not been peer-reviewed or been subject to the review by the NBER Board of Directors that accompanies official NBER publications.

kp.k: Widespread adoption exceeds intensive daily workplace use
kp.d: For pooled August and November 2024, 39.6 percent of working-age respondents report using generative AI overall; 26.5 percent of employed respondents report work use, 22.9 percent used it for work during the previous week, and 9.0 percent used it every workday. Figure 2 and the subsequent survey comparison report outside-work adoption of 33.7 percent, although Section 3 initially gives 35.5 percent for RPS outside-work use. ChatGPT leads product adoption at 28.1 percent of all respondents, followed by Gemini at 16.6 percent and embedded products such as Microsoft Copilot at 14.1 percent.
qs: The first bar shows that 39.6 percent of respondents report using genAI either at work or at home: 9.2 percent used it every day, 23.1 percent used it some but not all days, and 7.3 percent did not use it in the previous week.
We also find similar estimates of use for work (27.1 percent in the SWAA versus 26.5 percent in the RPS) and outside of work (35.5 percent in the SWAA versus 33.7 percent in the RPS).

kp.k: Independent survey comparison supports adoption estimates
kp.d: The authors fielded their module in December 2024 through the Survey of Working Arrangements and Attitudes (SWAA), using a different provider and applying the RPS weighting procedure. Among 4,698 respondents aged 20–64, overall adoption was 40.7 percent and workplace adoption 27.1 percent. They also compare ChatGPT use with YouGov and Pew surveys, while explicitly acknowledging possible selection on unobserved technological familiarity in online panels.
qs: The December 2024 wave (N = 4, 698) of the SWAA yields very similar rates of genAI usage to the RPS.
A potential concern with online-based surveys is that they may suffer from selection based on unobservable characteristics that are correlated with genAI use.

kp.k: Overall adoption outpaces computers and internet
kp.d: Relative to the authors’ chosen mass-market launch dates—IBM PC in 1981, commercial internet in 1995, and ChatGPT in 2022—generative AI adoption is faster overall than PC or internet adoption. Workplace adoption is similar: 27 percent for generative AI after two years versus 25 percent for PCs after three. The difference is driven by non-work adoption, at 34 percent versus 5 percent. The authors propose lower costs and greater user-friendliness as explanations, not established causal findings; internet data cannot distinguish work from non-work use.
qs: We find very similar work adoption rates for genAI after two years (27 percent) and PCs after three years (25 percent).
By contrast, Figure 4b reveals much higher non-work adoption rates for genAI (34 percent) compared with PCs (5 percent).
On the one hand, this means that similar adoption rates for PCs and genAI at work do not necessarily imply equivalent benefits from the two technologies.

kp.k: Early adoption broadly reproduces computer-era demographic patterns
kp.d: The authors find greater adoption among younger, more educated and higher-wage workers, resembling early PC adoption. Adoption rises with earnings until roughly the 80th percentile, then declines. Gender differs: generative AI use is higher among men, whereas early PC use was higher among women, which the authors associate with computer adoption in female-intensive administrative occupations. The source contains inconsistent gender magnitudes: Figure 5 shows generative AI adoption of 29.1 percent for men and 23.5 percent for women, while the accompanying prose says the gap is 7.5 percentage points.
qs: Both computer and genAI adoption have been faster for younger, more educated, and higher-wage workers.
Adoption rates increase steadily with income until roughly the 80th percentile, and then decline.

The one exception is gender: early genAI usage is higher for men, while computer usage was initially higher for women, reflecting rapid computer adoption among secretaries and other administrative occupations, which had large female shares.

kp.k: Higher user earnings do not establish causal benefits
kp.d: Controlling for demographic characteristics, education, occupation and industry, the authors report similar earnings associations for PC and generative AI use: 21 log points in weekly earnings, approximately 15 log points in hourly wages, and 5 log points in weekly hours. Daily generative AI users earn 40 percent more than non-users and weekly users 22 percent more; reported hourly wage differences are 30 percent and 15 percent respectively. The data cannot distinguish task composition, selection of more productive workers into adoption, or productivity effects caused by AI.
qs: Controlling for demographics, occupation, and industry, workers who used genAI every workday in the previous week earn 40 percent more than non-users, and workers who used it some but not all workdays earn 22 percent more than non-users.
Third, genAI may directly increase workers’ productivity and wages.
Our data do not allow us to distinguish between these explanations.

kp.k: Adoption spans occupations but remains uneven
kp.d: Workplace adoption is highest in computer/mathematical, management, and business/finance occupations at 43, 42 and 41 percent respectively, while all broad occupational groups fall between 15 and 50 percent. Industry adoption ranges from 58 percent in information services to 15 percent in leisure/accommodation/other services and 17 percent in transportation/utilities. Early adoption across occupations and industries correlates with early PC adoption at 0.66 and 0.71 respectively, but generative AI adoption is more broadly dispersed.
qs: genAI adoption at work is highest in computer and mathematical, management, and business and finance jobs (43, 42, and 41 percent respectively).
However, genAI use is broadly distributed, with every occupation group between 15 and 50 percent.
Overall, adoption rates by industry are highly correlated across the two technologies (ρ = 0.71).

kp.k: Task exposure predicts adoption imperfectly, including legal occupations
kp.d: Occupational adoption correlates at 0.67 with the task-based exposure measure from Eloundou, Manning, Mishkin and Rock (2024), offering partial validation of predicted exposure rather than equating exposure with adoption. Managers adopt more than predicted, while combined legal/social services and office/administration occupations adopt less. The authors suggest task-exposure measurement error, adoption costs or regulatory barriers as possible explanations; they do not establish which mechanism accounts for the legal/social services result.
qs: Our results offer partial validation of task-based exposure predictions, supporting the utility of these measures for researchers.

At the same time, managers have relatively high adoption rates relative to predicted exposure, while legal and social services and office and administration occupations have relatively low adoption rates.
Alternatively, they could reflect variation in adoption costs or regulatory barriers.

kp.k: Writing and information-handling tasks dominate reported usefulness
kp.d: Among users ranking tasks for helpfulness, 39.5 percent place writing communications in their top two, followed by administrative tasks at 25.6 percent, interpreting/translating/summarizing at 22.7 percent, and searching for facts or information at 18.0 percent. These are self-reported usefulness rankings, not measured task productivity or output quality. The authors find diverse uses, with eight of ten listed tasks ranked in the top two by at least 10 percent of users.
qs: The highest ranked tasks at work were writing (39.5 percent), administrative tasks (25.6 percent), interpreting/translating/summarizing text or data (22.7 percent), and searching for facts or information (18.0 percent).

While genAI seems most useful for creating, absorbing, and organizing written information or communications, eight of the ten tasks in our list were ranked in the top two by at least 10 percent of users, indicating a variety of use cases for genAI.

kp.k: Direct AI use occupies a minority of work hours
kp.d: Among workplace users, approximately 32 percent report an hour or more of active use on use days, 47 percent report 15–59 minutes, and 21 percent report under 15 minutes. More frequent users also tend to use AI longer each day. Using the more detailed November 2024 response categories to construct bounds, the authors estimate that AI assisted 6.0–24.9 percent of work hours among previous-week users, and 1.3–5.4 percent across all workers. These bounds measure direct use, not the share of tasks potentially exposed.
qs: Frequency and intensity of genAI use are positively correlated.
Among workers who use genAI, between 6.0 and 24.9 percent of all work hours were assisted by genAI.
Among all workers, between 1.3 and 5.4 percent of total work hours were assisted by genAI.

kp.k: Workers report time savings, varying substantially across occupations
kp.d: November 2024 respondents estimate how many additional hours the same work would have required without AI. The authors report average savings of 5.4 percent of work hours among users and 1.4 percent including non-users; 5.4 percent corresponds to 2.2 hours in a 40-hour week. Of previous-week users, 20.4 percent report saving four hours or more, rising to 33.3 percent among daily users. These are self-reported counterfactual savings rather than experimentally observed effects, and savings correlate with usage intensity across occupations and industries.
qs: We find an average time savings of 5.4 percent of work hours in the November 2024 wave.
When we include all workers, including non-users, workers saved 1.4 percent of total hours due to genAI.
Time savings and overall usage are highly correlated.

kp.k: Aggregate productivity estimates depend on converting savings into output
kp.d: A Cobb–Douglas model using November 2024 wages, hours and reported savings produces a 1.9 percent wage-weighted labor-productivity estimate and a 1.1 percent potential aggregate productivity gain after applying an AI-exposure-adjusted labor share of 0.57. Assumptions include unchanged capital, total factor productivity and hours, perfect substitution across workers, and redeployment of saved time into production. The authors caution that informal adoption may instead increase on-the-job leisure. Their cited firm-adoption estimate of 5.4 percent concerns February 2024, earlier than the worker surveys.
qs: If we assume an AI-exposure-adjusted labor share of 0.57, following Acemoglu (2024), the implied potential productivity gain is 1.1%.

If workers are now able to complete the same tasks in less time without their employer’s knowledge, they may take their time savings as on-the-job leisure, which would increase welfare but not productivity.
Thus we emphasize that these potential productivity gains from genAI may not show up in productivity statistics, at least for now.

kp.k: Model-implied gains resemble experimental estimates, with different horizons
kp.d: Using the midpoint of usage bounds, the authors estimate a wage-weighted AI-use share of 5.7 percent and infer a 33 percent productivity gain during AI-assisted hours, compared with an average 27 percent in cited randomized experiments. Their potential aggregate gain of 1.1 percent exceeds Acemoglu’s 0.7 percent estimate. They attribute the difference to assumed gains during use and adoption coverage: actual wage-weighted usage of 5.7 percent versus expert-assessed adoptable tasks of 4.6 percent. Their estimate concerns current usage, whereas Acemoglu’s gains develop over ten years.
qs: This implies that each hour spent using genAI increases the worker’s productivity for that hour by 33%.
Our estimate of the potential aggregate productivity gain from genAI of 1.1% is slightly higher than the estimate of 0.7% found by Acemoglu (2024).
A final difference is that Acemoglu (2024) assumes that these productivity gains would evolve gradually over the next ten years, whereas our estimates are based on current usage.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Bick, Blandin and Deming describe rapid but uneven adoption of generative AI across the U.S. economy, associated with reported time savings and conditional potential productivity gains.
pts.d: This is a cross-domain study, not a prediction about legal-service business models or lawyer displacement. Using pooled August and November 2024 survey results, the authors report overall adoption of 39.6% among working-age adults, workplace adoption of 26.5% among employed respondents, weekly workplace use of 22.9%, and daily workplace use of 9.0%. They conclude that overall adoption has been faster than adoption of PCs and the internet relative to their chosen mass-market launch dates, while workplace adoption resembles early PC adoption. They estimate that 1.3–5.4% of total work hours involved direct generative-AI use in November 2024. Users report average time savings of 5.4% of working hours, or 1.4% when non-users are included. Their model translates wage-weighted time savings into a potential aggregate productivity gain of approximately 1.1%. Writing, administrative work, interpretation, translation and summarization are prominent reported uses. Occupational exposure predictions correlate with actual adoption, but the combined legal/social-services group has relatively low adoption compared with predicted exposure. The authors suggest measurement differences, adoption costs or regulatory barriers as possible explanations, rather than establishing a legal-sector mechanism.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The claims rest on weighted worker surveys, historical adoption comparisons, occupational correlations and a production-model calculation—not a causal measurement of economy-wide productivity.
pts.d: The February 2025 revision pools more than 10,000 initial responses to the August and November 2024 Real-Time Population Survey, with final analysis samples of 9,742 adults and 6,951 employed respondents. The online Qualtrics panel is nonrandom; the authors target demographic composition and weight observations against the Current Population Survey. They validate adoption findings with a December 2024 Survey of Working Arrangements and Attitudes module and compare ChatGPT uptake with other surveys. Historical comparisons use CPS computer/internet supplements and ITU internet data. Occupational adoption correlates 0.67 with predicted exposure from Eloundou and colleagues. Usage-hour bounds and reported time savings rely on November data. The 1.1% productivity estimate combines self-reported counterfactual time savings, wages and hours with a Cobb-Douglas production model and an exposure-adjusted labor share of 0.57. A model-implied 33% productivity gain during AI-assisted hours is compared with a 27% average from cited experiments; it is not an experimental result from this study. Wage differences between users and non-users are associations whose causal explanation the authors cannot identify. The source is an NBER working paper explicitly described as not peer-reviewed.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The principal findings concern late-2024 adoption and potential gains at current usage levels; realized productivity and longer-run effects remain conditional.
pts.d: The paper was issued in September 2024 and revised in February 2025. Main adoption estimates pool August and November 2024; detailed usage bounds and time savings come from November, with independent-panel validation in December. Historical diffusion comparisons date mass-market availability to the IBM PC in 1981, commercial internet availability in 1995, and ChatGPT in November 2022. These comparisons depend on those reference dates and do not establish equivalent economic benefits: cheaper AI adoption may support faster diffusion without implying the same value as earlier technologies. The potential productivity calculation assumes saved time becomes additional production, unchanged capital, total factor productivity and working hours, competitive wages reflecting marginal productivity, and perfect substitutability of labor across workers. Gains may instead become on-the-job leisure, increasing welfare without measured output. Imperfect substitution could reduce aggregate gains. The authors distinguish their current-usage estimate from Acemoglu's ten-year projection and do not offer a definite long-run forecast.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: Adoption and reported benefits vary across working-age adults, occupations and industries, with greater uptake among younger, more educated and higher-paid workers.
pts.d: The main population is U.S. adults aged 18–64, with workplace results restricted to employed respondents. Computer/mathematical, management, and business/finance occupations lead workplace adoption at approximately 43%, 42%, and 41%, respectively; information services leads industries at 58%. The authors nevertheless find use across every broad occupational group. Computer/mathematical and management workers report saving approximately 2.1–2.5% of hours when non-users are included, compared with 0.4% in personal services. Information services reports 2.6% time savings, compared with 0.6% in leisure, accommodation and other services. More intensive users earn more after controls, but the paper does not show that AI caused those wage differences. Employers may benefit if worker time savings become additional output, while workers may benefit through reduced effort or leisure. Legal occupations are grouped with social services for the relevant comparisons; no separate conclusion is established about law firms, in-house departments, clients, access to justice or legal employment displacement.
